newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - AEA pledges "progressive" div policy.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - AEA pledges "progressive" div policy.

text.p: AEA Technology Plc, the science and research group which may be the very last privatisation of Britain's Conservative government, is promising potential investors "a progressive and reasonable" dividend policy.
In a telephone interview with Reuters, AEA chief executive Peter Watson declined to give explicit forecasts for payouts to shareholders, but said: "We know the City will require a reasonable policy."
AEA, which is a spin-off from the Atomic Energy Authority, is expected to raise around 200 million stg for government coffers. Watson said this estimate "is not far out".

Watson was speaking after the publication of the pathfinder prospectus for AEA Technology, which specializes in offering safety, engineering, consultancy and computer services to the nuclear industry in the U.K. and overseas.
The placing is due to commence on September 25, with dealing on the London Stock Exchange beginning on September 26.

The chief executive declined to give specific forecasts for the group's sales and profits for the current year ending in March 1997. But he said the group is "ahead of last year on sales and profits," and that it is telling potential investors "we are showing improvements and we expect that to continue."
AEA Technology posted operating profit of 19.8 million stg in the year ended March 31, 1996, on sales of 253.3 million.

There has been some controversry over the government's decision to keep a so-called "golden share" in AEA Technology, which would allow it to veto any unwelcome takeover approaches, for just three years.

Golden shares in previous privatizations have tended to be kept in place for five years, and opposition politicians have pointed to the sensitive nature of much of AEA Technology's work, which includes monitoring the safety of Britain's nuclear submarines.
"A lot of private sector companies are in very sensitive areas. We'll be no different from them," Watson said.
He said the possibility of takeover approaches from other companies "is not an issue. I don't think it's a problem."
The U.K. government accounted for 46 percent of AEA Technology sales in the year ended March 1996, with other U.K. pubic sector bodies representing 14 percent and the private sector 19 percent.
Watson told Reuters the group's aim is to increase the proportion of business from overseas to around one-third over the next four to five years, from just over 20 percent.
"We see quite a lot of growth there and in the private sector and expect to retain our government business at about the same level," he said.
AEA Technology already has operations in the U.S., where it assists in cleaning up chemical weapons sites, and in Japan, where it works with two of the country's biggest nuclear power generators.
Watson joted that the company does not have the scope for cost-cutting which has characterized previous privatizations and been a major source of profit growth.
He said most of AEA Technology's cost-cutting "is behind us, with the workforce reduced to around 3,500 from 4,600 over the past two years."
The chief executive also repeated a pledge that executives will not receive special treatment in the form of share options, with benefits shared across all employees.
Watson said around five percent of profits each year will be used to buy shares for all staff.
-- Jonathan Birt, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
